title: Dropbox File Storage: Complete Architecture
description: Design a cloud file synchronization and storage system with 4MB chunking, content-addressable storage, delta sync, and conflict resolution.

data.text: Design a cloud storage and synchronization service like Dropbox or Google Drive. The system allows 700+ million users to store files, sync changes seamlessly across multiple desktop and mobile devices, share folders with granular permissions, and roll back to previous file revisions. The central engineering challenge is bandwidth optimization and reliability: a minor edit to a 1GB video or presentation must only transmit the modified bytes (Delta Sync), files must be split into deduplicated content-addressed blocks, and concurrent offline edits must resolve gracefully.

terms.definition: Storing data blocks where the storage key/identifier is the cryptographic SHA-256 hash of the block payload itself.
Detecting and transmitting only the modified 4MB chunks of an edited file rather than re-uploading the entire file across the network.
The storage subsystem responsible for receiving, encrypting, deduplicating, and persisting raw 4MB binary file chunks into cloud object stores.
The transactional database managing user accounts, directory structures, file versions, sharing permissions, and the ordered list of chunk hashes for each file.
The client daemon monitoring filesystem events (FSEvents/inotify), computing block hashes, and synchronizing state with the cloud.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: File Upload & Download: Store files up to 50GB with resumable chunked streaming
Automatic Cross-Device Sync: Real-time synchronization across desktop (macOS/Windows/Linux), web, and mobile devices
Delta Sync & Deduplication: Only upload new or modified 4MB chunks; eliminate identical chunks across the entire system
Revision History: Automatic versioning with 30-day (free) or unlimited (enterprise) rollback capability
Sharing & Permissions: Share folders/files with Read or Read/Write access; generate public links with expiry
Offline Editing & Conflict Resolution: Allow offline changes and generate branching conflict files if concurrent edits clash

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Scale: 700M+ registered users; 100M+ daily active; 500+ Petabytes of total stored data
Durability: 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability via geographic multi-region replication and erasure coding
Bandwidth Efficiency: Delta sync and client-side compression to minimize mobile and broadband data usage
Latency: File sync notifications dispatched to peer devices in under 500ms over persistent WebSockets
Consistency: Strong consistency for metadata operations (file list, versions, and chunk order)

data.text: The architecture strictly decouples the high-volume data plane (Block Storage of binary chunks) from the high-consistency control plane (Metadata Service, Notification Service, and Sync Gateway).

data.text: When a user edits a file, the client splits it into 4MB chunks and hashes each chunk. The client sends only the list of hashes to the server. If 9 out of 10 hashes already exist in the cloud, only the single altered chunk is uploaded.

faqs.question: How is global deduplication achieved across different users?
faqs.answer: Chunks are stored in Content-Addressable Storage (CAS) keyed by `SHA256(chunk_payload)`. If User A and User B both save the same 200MB installer or presentation, the chunk hashes are identical. The Block Service detects the hash already exists and increments a reference counter in the metadata DB without storing duplicate bytes, saving petabytes of storage.

faqs.question: How are concurrent offline edits resolved without data loss?
faqs.answer: Dropbox uses a Last-Write-Wins with Conflicted Copy strategy. If User A and User B edit the same file while offline, whichever user commits to the Metadata Service first wins the original filename. When the second user reconnects and attempts to commit revision N, the server detects a revision conflict and saves the second user's file as `Document (John's conflicted copy 2026-10-02).docx`.

faqs.question: Why separate the Metadata Database from the Block Storage?
faqs.answer: Metadata requires strict ACID consistency, sub-10ms transactional reads/writes, and relational queries for directory traversal. Binary file chunks are immutable, write-once blobs that require cheap, horizontally scalable durability (S3/erasure-coded disks). Combining them would cripple database performance.

faqs.question: How does client sync handle poor mobile connections?
faqs.answer: The client sync daemon uses an exponential backoff retry queue with chunk checkpointing. If an upload fails midway through a 500MB file (e.g. after uploading chunk 42 of 125), the client resumes from chunk 43 when connection restores without restarting the entire file upload.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: 4MB chunking with SHA-256 signatures enables both intra-file delta sync and global cross-user deduplication
Decoupled architecture: Block Servers manage raw binary data while Metadata Servers enforce ACID directory state
Client-side Local Indexer (SQLite + OS filesystem watcher) detects changes and hashes chunks before hitting network
WebSocket Notification Gateways wake up peer devices instantaneously when file revisions commit
Conflicted copy branching prevents silent data overwrites during concurrent offline modifications
data.takeaway: Dropbox achieves extreme bandwidth efficiency and 11-nines reliability by treating files as immutable content-addressed chunk chains, ensuring only modified blocks travel across the wire.
